title: Ephemeral session anchoring and probabilistic traffic drainer for active-active edge
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: Implement an active-active failover mechanism at the hosted API edge that preserves session and streaming continuity where possible while allowing controlled, measurable traffic shifts between regions.

Motivation: Current abrupt region drains cause token/KV cache loss and long-running streaming interruptions. We need mechanisms that (1) limit SLO regressions during failover, (2) allow gradual traffic migration with session-friendly semantics, and (3) provide clear circuit-breaker and load-shedding levers when downstream capacity is constrained.

Proposed approach:
- Ephemeral session anchoring: issue short-lived session anchor tokens (anchor_id) bound to region/edge instance. Anchors are cheap, signed tokens that reference a small metadata set (client_id, last_kv_seq, preferred_region_hint). They allow a controlled transfer path for session state and enable downstream honor/lookup without full KV sync for most cases.
- Probabilistic traffic drainer: instead of binary drain, use a probability-based shift schedule. For each epoch (configurable, default 10s) increase fractional egress to target region by X% (configurable ramp, e.g., +5% per epoch). Clients with active anchors may be preferentially kept on origin until a safe handoff threshold is reached.
- Streaming continuity heuristics: for streaming sessions with active KV cache, implement a short-lived in-memory cache checkpoint + anchor handshake. When we shift a streaming session, the origin will publish an ephemeral checkpoint reference and the anchor token allows the destination to fetch the minimal delta via the checkpoint service.
- Circuit breakers and load shedding: SLO-driven circuit breakers at three levels: edge (region-wide overload), gateway (per-model queue depth), and tenant (per-api-key throughput). Circuit triggers: sustained 95th/99th latency breaches, queue depth above threshold, or GPU utilization > 92% for N seconds. Load shedding policy: tiered degradation—(1) reject best-effort endpoints first, (2) reduce max tokens/response, (3) probabilistic request dropping for non-anchor requests, (4) fallback to cheaper model variant.
- Telemetry and SLOs: instrument anchor handoffs, percent of anchored vs unanchored sessions shifted, handoff success/failure rates, streaming reattachment latency. SLO targets: 99.9% non-streaming request availability within region, 99.5% for streaming continuity across a planned shift window; latency 95th < 150ms overall during canary ramp.

Trade-offs considered:
- Anchor tokens add an indirection and small auth overhead; mitigated by signing and short TTLs.
- Probabilistic drain increases complexity in routing logic and observability but reduces abrupt session loss at scale.
- Checkpointing for streaming adds storage read/write paths; plan to keep deltas tiny (only KV differences) and TTL them aggressively.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Design & schema for anchor token (signing, fields, TTL) + ACL model for anchor acceptance.
2) Small state service: ephemeral checkpoint store (S3 with short TTL or in-memory cache backed by Redis) and handshake endpoints.
3) Router changes: support per-request anchor evaluation and probabilistic egress decisions. Add control plane API for ramp schedules and emergency drain.
4) Circuit breaker integration: reuse existing breakout signals; parameterize thresholds per-region/tenant.
5) Observability: dashboards for anchor metrics, ramp progress, SLO heatmap, and incident playbook links.
6) Tests: unit tests, integration tests with synthetic long-lived streams, chaos-tests (region kill) in staging.
7) Canary rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 60% -> 100% over multiple cycles with SLO gating and automatic rollback on regressions.

Rollout safety:
- Gate each ramp step on canary SLOs (latency, error budget burn, stream reattach success).
- Emergency circuit: full rollback of routing policy within 10s via control plane and immediate throttling fallback to origin.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Anchor token TTL optimal value for long streaming sessions (default 5m vs 30m?)
- Checkpoint delta format and max size (to avoid heavy cross-region copy)
- Whether to persist checkpoints to S3 or use ephemeral redis clusters per-region (cost vs reliability)

Acceptance criteria:
- Anchor token defined and implemented with signing and TTL enforcement.
- Router can perform probabilistic egress decisions with configurable epoch/ramp.
- Streaming handoff proof-of-concept: at least 90% of simulated long streams reattach within 3s during a 30% traffic shift.
- Circuit breaker triggers integrated and cause expected load-shedding behavior in chaos tests.
- Observability dashboards displaying ramp progress and SLO gating metrics.
- Runbook updated and security review completed.
comments: 2025-02-11 - Aisha Patel: Kickoff meeting notes attached. Decided to prototype anchors as JWTs with a small payload; security to review signing key rotation.
2025-02-18 - Lucas Meyer: Completed router plugin prototype that can do probabilistic egress based on per-epoch RNG. Initial perf impact minimal (~0.5ms p50).
2025-02-24 - Priya Rao (SRE): Circuit-breaker thresholds proposed: region_util>92% for 20s, queue_depth>1000 for 30s. Need to calibrate with staging load tests.
2025-02-28 - Design review: Agreed streaming checkpoint should include seq ranges and hash to verify integrity. Decision: use Redis ephemeral with optional S3 fallback.
2025-03-03 - Security (J. Kim): Requesting formal threat model for anchor tokens and signing key rotation plan. Added to dependencies.
2025-03-05 - Lucas Meyer: Integration tests passing on staging. Observability panels created: anchor-handshake, ramp-progress, streaming-reattach-latency. Preparing canary 1% tomorrow.

Router supports configurable probabilistic ramp and epoch tuning.
Streaming handoff POC achieves >=90% reattach success within 3s at 30% shift in staging.
Circuit-breaker triggers cause documented load-shedding sequence in chaos tests.
